summary: Fort Jones occupies barely six-tenths of a square mile in Scott Valley, a broad, flat agricultural basin walled in by the Marble Mountains to the west and the Scott Mountains to the south — a setting that delivers wide-sky sunsets over serious wilderness without requiring a single switchback to get home. With just 668 residents, the town functions less as a self-contained economy and more as a rural outpost where ranching, timber, and public-sector jobs (county services, the U.S. Forest Service) anchor most livelihoods; switching employers likely means driving to Yreka, about 25 miles northeast on Highway 3. A median home value around $213,000 against a median household income of roughly $43,400 yields a price-to-income ratio near 4.9 — more accessible than much of California, though a poverty rate above 28% signals that the local wage base is thin. Summers bring long, bright days averaging nearly nine hours of sunshine and comfortable highs, while winter nights regularly dip below freezing in the valley's cold-air pool. The Klamath National Forest and the Marble Mountain Wilderness sit practically at the doorstep, offering trail access that most California towns can only advertise as a weekend drive. Fort Jones is a place where affordability and extraordinary landscape access come packaged with genuine economic isolation — the tradeoff is the entire point.
